title: In saving faith distinguish the direct act (embracing Christ) from the reflex act (recognizing one’s faith)
source_text: XXVIII. Imo quamvis, ut jam probatum est, certa illa persuasio, quam fidelis habere potest de remissione peccatorum suorum, & sua cum Deo per Christum reconciliatione, non sit formalis actus fidei justificantis, aliqua tamen ratione pro fidei illius actu haberi potest. Quod ut intelligatur, in fide salutari atque justificante duplex actus distinguendus est. Unus directus, atque primarius. Alter reflexus & secundarius. Directus est ille quo fidelis Christum, ut Redemptorem & Servatorem nostrum, agnoscit atque amplectitur, & in eo salutem & justitiam quaerit. Reflexus vero ille est quo fidelis in propriam fidem reflectitur, eamque recognoscit; illiusque effecta, timorem, videlicet, & dilectionem Dei, & charitatem erga proximum, in corde suo sentit & experitur. Unde colligit se Christo vere insertum esse, ejusque gratiae & beneficiorum revera participem.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed although, as already proved, that certain persuasion which a believer can have concerning the remission of his sins and his reconciliation with God through Christ is not the formal act of justifying faith, yet in some way it can be held as an act of that faith. That this may be understood, in saving and justifying faith a twofold act is to be distinguished. One direct and primary. The other reflex and secondary. The direct is that by which the believer acknowledges and embraces Christ as our Redeemer and Savior and seeks salvation and righteousness in him. The reflex is that by which the believer turns back upon his own faith and recognizes it, and senses and experiences in his heart its effects—namely fear and love of God and charity toward neighbor. From which he gathers that he is truly inserted into Christ and truly a partaker of his grace and benefits.
pass_b_english: Assurance is not justifying faith’s formal act, yet may be called a reflex secondary act of that faith.
The direct act embraces Christ; the reflex act reads one’s own faith and its fruits.
